schema.headline: The Mozart Effect Is a Myth, and Here's What Happened
schema.description: Does listening to Mozart make you smarter? You've probably heard that it does: play classical music to a baby and you build a sharper brain, put the right sonata on before an exam and you score higher.

faq.q: So does Mozart actually make you smarter, or not?
faq.a: Not in the way the headline says. The original 1993 study (Rauscher, Shaw & Ky, Nature) found a small bump on one spatial-reasoning task in thirty-six students that was gone in about fifteen minutes, and Rauscher herself later said it never showed Mozart makes you smarter. When Pietschnig and colleagues (2010) pooled nearly forty studies and more than three thousand people, the Mozart-specific advantage basically vanished once you compared it against any other stimulating thing (d dropped from about 0.37 versus silence to about 0.15). That's why the popular claim grades an F.

faq.q: If the lab effect was real, why does the "myth" label still apply?
faq.a: Because two different claims got tangled. The short-term arousal-and-mood bump is real, since lively music can lift your alertness for a stretch, and that can carry into a task. What's false is the specific, durable, makes-you-smarter-for-life version that got sold to a generation of parents, built on top of a narrow lab blip that was real.

faq.q: What was actually doing the work, then?
faq.a: Arousal and mood rather than Mozart. A lively piece of music warms up the brain the same way coffee or a good story does. The moment you put Mozart next to anything else that perks you up, the two come out even. The active ingredient was being a bit more alert than the people sitting in silence. Thinking clearly about what music is really doing to people in a room is the work I do. The evidence grade for this one is an F.
